claim: Gyldayn is framed as an extremely unreliable narrator, and that distance keeps readers from investing in characters who rarely stay long enough to be known.
source: Patrick Nugent, The Irish Times, 16 Feb 2019
page: Fire and Blood review: Don't expect a novel

verdict.trueWording: It's hard to root for anyone as they rarely stick around
verdict.note: Quote 'an extremely unreliable narrator' is verbatim ("purportedly written by Archmaester Gyldayn, an extremely unreliable narrator"), and the not-investing limb is on the page ("It's hard to root for anyone as they rarely stick around long enough for us to get to know them"). But the review attributes that difficulty to the events' density, not to narratorial distance; the two facts sit in adjacent sentences with no causal link drawn.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the causal limb 'that distance keeps readers from investing' - Nugent attributes the failure to root to characters not sticking around, never to the unreliable narrator's distance

claim: The roundup links the Independent, Publishers Weekly, GQ, The Times, the Sunday Times, Tor.com and Mental Floss; it does not link NYT, Guardian or Vox reviews, and none were found.
source: Winter Is Coming critics roundup, 23 Nov 2018
page: What are the critics saying about Fire & Blood?

verdict.trueWording: links Independent, PW, GQ, The Times, Sunday Times, Tor.com, Mental Floss
verdict.note: The link set is exactly right, confirmed by parsing every href in the raw HTML: independent.co.uk (O'Connor), publishersweekly.com/978-1-5247-9628-0, gq-magazine.co.uk/article/fire-and-blood-review, thetimes.co.uk (Rifkind), thetimes.co.uk/magazine (Dan Jones, Sunday Times), tor.com/2018/11/21, mentalfloss.com - and no nytimes.com, theguardian.com or vox.com link anywhere on the page. The final limb is the problem: a roundup page cannot attest that no such reviews exist or that a search failed to find them. WebSearch could not settle it either (those three domains are blocked to the agent), so the limb stays unverified rather than contradicted.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'and none were found' - an assertion about the researcher's own search, which the roundup page cannot support either way

claim: Even the summary voice lands concrete, countable images, such as a dragon devouring a queen in six bites.
quote: devoured the queen in six bites

verdict.trueWording: Brief sections are dramatic ('the golden dragon devoured the queen in six bites')
verdict.note: Quote is verbatim on the raw PW page, but the review assigns that image to the BRIEF DRAMATIC sections and explicitly contrasts them with summary: 'they only last a few pages before a return to brisk summary.' The page does not say the summary voice lands such images; it says the opposite relation.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the SUMMARY voice lands these concrete images - the review credits them to brief dramatic sections set against 'brisk summary'

claim: The Jaehaerys excerpt dates its action to a regnal year (58 AC) and advances by chronology rather than by scene.
source: George R.R. Martin, Not a Blog excerpt post, 27 Sep 2018
page: A FIRE & BLOOD Excerpt just for YOU!

verdict.unsupportedLimb: advances by chronology rather than by scene — the excerpt renders full dramatised scenes with dialogue
verdict.trueWording: plans were laid in 58 AC for Jaehaerys and Alysanne
verdict.note: Quote "plans were laid in 58 AC" is verbatim (once, mid-sentence, not as a sentence opener despite the feature label 'regnal-year sentence openers'). 58 AC is the only regnal year in the entire excerpt; later transitions are relative ('A few days later', 'After taking leave of White Harbor', 'The longer the queen stayed'). The second limb fails: the excerpt descends into extended scenes at Winterfell built from direct dialogue (Alaric Stark's "I hope you brought something warmer than that", the exchange at the Wall), which the sibling claim 364 itself asserts.

claim: Because Gyldayn 'writes' the book, Martin says it makes sense he would not have all the information, and its mysteries are possible answers, not definitive ones.
source: Winter Is Coming digest of Martin's Not a Blog comments, 3 May 2018
quote: he wouldn't have all the information
page: George R.R. Martin clears up misconceptions about Fire & Blood

verdict.unsupportedLimb: Martin says it makes sense he would not have all the information — that sentence is the Winter Is Coming writer's own gloss, not a Martin quote
verdict.trueWording: it is all possible answers, not meant to be definitive
verdict.note:
Quote "he wouldn't have all the information" is verbatim on the page, but I checked the raw HTML: it sits in the article's own

body paragraph ("Fire & Blood is 'written' by Archmaester Gyldayn of the Citadel, so it makes sense that he wouldn't have all the information."), authored by Dan Selcke — NOT inside the adjacent

carrying Martin's words. The second limb IS Martin verbatim in that blockquote: "in the case of things like Valyria and the dragon eggs, it is all possible answers, not meant to be definitive." So the mysteries limb verifies and the attribution limb does not.

claim: Archaic markers ('whilst', 'alarum', 'a moon's turn', 'the hour of the bat/owl') set the register without heavy Latinate vocabulary.
source: George R.R. Martin, 'The Princess and the Queen' excerpt (primary text), Reactor/Tor.com
page: Dangerous Women: The Princess and The Queen (Excerpt)

verdict.unsupportedLimb: without heavy Latinate vocabulary — the excerpt's opening sentence is "the savage internecine struggle for the Iron Throne"
verdict.trueWording: at the hour of the bat; a general alarum; a moon's turn
verdict.note: All four archaic markers verify verbatim: "whilst"/"Whilst", "without raising a general alarum", "for a fortnight or a moon's turn", "at the hour of the bat" and "It was the hour of the owl." The negative limb is the failure: the same excerpt reaches for markedly Latinate diction — "savage internecine struggle", "strikes us as grotesquely inappropriate", "two principal claimants", "became embroiled" — so the page does not support 'without heavy Latinate vocabulary' as stated.

claim: A king's death is dated to the day and moon of a year and to a named hour, precision that reads as record rather than scene.
source: George R.R. Martin, 'The Princess and the Queen' excerpt (primary text), Reactor/Tor.com
page: Dangerous Women: The Princess and The Queen (Excerpt)

verdict.unsupportedLimb: the named hour dates the discovery of the body, not the death — "His body was discovered by a serving man at the hour of the bat"
verdict.trueWording: on the third day of third moon of 129 AC
verdict.note: "third day of third moon" is verbatim, in "the conflict burst into the open on the third day of third moon of 129 AC, when the ailing, bedridden King Viserys I Targaryen closed his eyes for a nap in the Red Keep of King's Landing, and died without waking." Day, moon and year all present. But the page attaches no hour to the death itself: the hour of the bat marks the serving man's discovery of the body, and "It was the hour of the owl" marks the summoning of the small council. The calendar-precision reading holds; the specific limb dating the death to a named hour does not.

claim: Gyldayn's line on the dragon Tessarion shows the chronicler's habit of closing an unknowable with a rhetorical question.
source: A Wiki of Ice and Fire, 'Gyldayn'
quote: Who can know the heart of a dragon?
page: Gyldayn - A Wiki of Ice and Fire

verdict.trueWording: "Who can know the heart of a dragon?" - Gyldayn writing about Tessarion
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that this is the chronicler's HABIT - the page carries exactly one such line (a single entry in its Quotes section) and says nothing about a recurring pattern of closing unknowables with rhetorical questions
verdict.note: Same AWOIAF capture. The quote and its attribution to Gyldayn writing about Tessarion are verbatim on the page (Quotes section, cited to Fire & Blood, 'The Dying of the Dragons - Rhaenyra Overthrown'). The generalisation to a habit is an inference the page does not evidence, so the claim is graded PARTIAL rather than verified.

claim: Martin kills off central characters who are richly imagined, three-dimensional portraits, which most writers could not bear to lose.
source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
quote: richly imagined, textured, three-dimensional portraits of central characters

verdict.trueWording: the kind many writers couldn't bear to kill off
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'most writers' — the page says 'many writers', not most
verdict.note: Quote 'richly imagined, textured, three-dimensional portraits of central characters' is verbatim on the LRB page, in the paragraph listing Renly, Tywin, Robb and Joffrey ('He dies' x4), closing 'the kind many writers couldn't bear to kill off. Nobody needs to give Martin any advice about how he needs to slaughter his darlings.' The kill-off limb and the three-dimensional-portrait limb are fully supported; only the quantifier is inflated from 'many' to 'most'.

claim: The Bran defenestration lands harder in the book than on screen because Bran has already been established as a viewpoint character.
source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
quote: even more of an impact, perhaps

verdict.trueWording: equivalent impact in the books; even more of an impact, perhaps
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the flat comparative 'lands harder in the book than on screen' — Lanchester hedges ('equivalent impact ... even more of an impact, perhaps')
verdict.note: Page: 'It has an equivalent impact in the books; even more of an impact, perhaps, because Bran has already been established as one of the characters from whose viewpoint the story is told.' The causal limb (already a viewpoint character) is verbatim-supported; the claim strips the source's hedge and asserts the comparison outright.

claim: The three-walled description of Qarth (animals, war, sex) reads as a sly reference to the series' own layered decor.
source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
quote: a sly reference to the series itself

verdict.trueWording: in the Qartheen decor a sly reference to the series itself
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'the series' own layered decor' — Mendelsohn grounds the joke in the epic's 'slowly metastasizing' length (trilogy to five of a projected seven, each ~1,000 pages), not in any decor of the series
verdict.note: The quoted Qarth passage does run animals (outer red sandstone), war (middle grey granite) and sex (innermost black marble), so the three-walled/animals-war-sex limb is exactly right, and 'a sly reference to the series itself' is verbatim. What the page does not say is that the referent is the series' decor; the tenor of the comparison there is scale — 'anyone familiar with Martin's slowly metastasizing epic—it began as a trilogy in 1996 and now runs to five volumes of a projected seven, each around a thousand pages long—will find it hard not to see in the Qartheen decor a sly reference to the series itself.'

claim: Martin's taste for pageantry and colour (his medieval miniature dioramas) carries into the fiction.
source: Laura Miller, 'Just Write It!', The New Yorker, 11 Apr 2011
quote: I like the pageantry and the color

verdict.trueWording: I like the pageantry and the color - said of his medieval miniatures
verdict.note: Quote verbatim, and the dioramas of mostly medieval miniatures are on the page. But the page never says this taste carries into the fiction: the only bridge it draws from the closets to the novels is population - 'Like his closets, Martin's head is crammed with people' - leading to Garcia's thousand-name census, not to pageantry or colour in the prose.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the pageantry-and-colour taste carries into the fiction

claim: The plotty, cliffhangery reversals (dead! alive! dying! a zombie! in disguise!) are conceded as the selling point.
source: Sady Doyle, 'Enter Ye Myne Mystic World of Gayng-Raype', Tiger Beatdown, 26 Aug 2011
quote: the plotty, cliffhangery aspects of Martin’s writing

verdict.trueWording: I could acknowledge the plotty, cliffhangery aspects as a selling point
verdict.note: Wayback raw capture of tigerbeatdown.com (live host refuses connection). Quote and the whole reversal list are verbatim: 'I could acknowledge the plotty, cliffhangery aspects of Martin's writing as a selling point: So-and-so was dead! But now he's alive! But now he's dying! But now he's a zombie! But now he's the Prince of Sblarghlhaar, because he was IN DISGUISE!' But it sits in a run of declined moves ('I could get into the reasons... I could try to construct some kind of nuanced argument... I could try to look at the positives, before I get to the criticism. But you know what? I'm still going to criticize the books'), so the concession is hypothetical and withheld, and the article is 'a selling point', not 'the'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: conceded as the selling point — the page frames it as a hypothetical 'I could acknowledge... as a selling point' that Doyle then declines

claim: The essay's core objection is the count of gratuitous rape, molestation and domestic-violence scenes, tallied book by book.
source: Sady Doyle, 'Enter Ye Myne Mystic World of Gayng-Raype', Tiger Beatdown, 26 Aug 2011

verdict.trueWording: creepy primarily for his gratuitous rape/molestation/DV scenes
verdict.note: Wayback raw capture. The core-objection limb is verbatim: 'He is creepy, primarily, because of his TWENTY THOUSAND MILLION GRATUITOUS RAPE AND/OR MOLESTATION AND/OR DOMESTIC VIOLENCE SCENES. And I could write a post about those... But you know what would be easier? I could just count them. One by one by one.' The essay does walk the books in order (sections 1-4, each with a 'Major Female Characters' roster), but no per-book count of scenes exists: the arithmetic is one cumulative 'FINAL SCORES' block after book four counting characters, not scenes — '83%' of major female characters abused/raped/threatened, '100%' of the female children.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: tallied book by book — the tallies are a single cumulative FINAL SCORES block (percentages of major female characters), not a per-book count of scenes

claim: Compounds like sellsword, smallfolk, ironborn, greenseer and weirwood are a highly creative and enjoyable aspect of the style.
source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
quote: a highly creative and enjoyable aspect of his style

verdict.trueWording: Martin uses this facility to coin scores of neologisms (of the compounds)
verdict.note: The quote is verbatim but belongs to section 6 'New coinages', whose examples are sept/septon/septa, maester, wildlings, pyromancer, holdfast, warg, damphair. The five words the claim names are all on the page but in the SEPARATE section 7 'New word combinations', where the page says only 'Martin uses this facility to coin scores of neologisms' and that they 'build up a linguistic base for the otherness of his fantasy world' - no creative/enjoyable praise. Confirmed positionally: the praise phrase is on text line 73 under heading '6 New coinages'; the compound list is on line 77 under '7 New word combinations'. (The sibling 2013 post does call the compounds 'scores of wonderful and evocative neologisms' - see index 507 - but that is a different page from the one cited here.)
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the praise 'a highly creative and enjoyable aspect of his style' is said of the new coinages (sept, maester, warg), not of the compounds sellsword/smallfolk/ironborn/greenseer/weirwood

claim: Repeated 'cool' and 'still' in the Water Gardens passage may be haste or deliberate torpor-evoking repetition.
source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
quote: signs of haste, or careful repetitions

verdict.trueWording: the word paintings of the Water Palace of Lord Martell of Dorne
verdict.note: Substantive limb is verbatim: '(I can't decide whether the repetitions in this passage - of cool and still - are signs of haste, or careful repetitions designed to evoke the lazy, torpid atmosphere of Lord Martell's sea retreat.)' Haste-vs-deliberate-torpor and the two repeated words are exactly right. Only the location label diverges: the page introduces the quoted FFC40 passage as the 'Water Palace', never 'Water Gardens'. Relabel the passage and the claim is fully sourced.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'the Water Gardens passage' - the page calls it the 'Water Palace of Lord Martell of Dorne'
